0.title: Widgets
0.content: A widget puts live data on the dashboard. There are two kinds, as in homepage: . | Service widgets go on a service’s card in services.yaml, under widget: (or widgets: for several). They show the numbers of that service: the queue of Radarr, the blocked queries of Pi-hole, the VMs of Proxmox. # services.yaml - Media: - Radarr: href: http://radarr.lan icon: radarr.svg widget: type: radarr url: http://radarr.lan:7878 key: "{{DASHBOARD_VAR_RADARR_KEY}}" . | Header widgets go in the page’s header, in widgets.yaml: the date and time, system resources, search, the weather. # widgets.yaml - openmeteo: label: Amsterdam latitude: 52.37 longitude: 4.89 . | . Every widget below comes from the widgets collection, which is always installed. Missing one? Any widget package can be added under plugins:: the Catalogue lists packages by others, and Extend shows how to write your own.

4.title: Configuration
4.content: All configuration lives in one folder (/config in the container, --config or DASHBOARD_CONFIG_DIR otherwise). Every file is optional. The page reloads by itself when a .yaml file changes. On a network share (NFS, SMB) changes made on another machine are not noticed; set DASHBOARD_WATCH_POLL to a number of seconds to check the files that often instead. Problems are shown at the top of the page with the file and a path into it. A broken entry is skipped and the rest keeps working. Coming from homepage? Its configuration works as it is: see From homepage. | File | What | . | settings.yaml | Title, language, theme, layout per group, tabs, discovery interval, plugins, providers (keys and logins for widgets) | . | bookmarks.yaml | Groups of links | . | widgets.yaml | Widgets in the header | . | services.yaml | Groups of services; filters hide a card or widget while all is well | . | kubernetes.yaml | Kubernetes discovery | . | docker.yaml | Docker servers (status and discovery) | . | proxmox.yaml | Proxmox nodes (VM and container status) | . | other .yaml files | Pulled in with !include (see Including other files) | . | icons/ | Your own icons, used as icon: /icons/name.svg (see Images) | . | custom.css, custom.js | Your own style and script, loaded after the page’s own | . | plugins/ | Managed by the dashboard: downloaded widgets and plugins.lock.yaml. Older versions and removed sources are deleted after each sync | .

5.title: First start
5.content: The image starts the setup wizard when /config is empty: it writes the file .onboarding, and while that is there the page opens at /setup. The wizard has five steps: . | Basics: title, language, theme and colour (settings.yaml). | Docker: the Docker servers it can reach (a mounted socket, or docker.yaml once there is one), each with its version and number of containers, or the error it got; a socket it may not use gets a hint (start the container as root, the default, or use a socket proxy). Add a socket path or the host:port of a docker-socket-proxy or Docker API, and it is checked at once; what you add is written to docker.yaml, with the mounted socket. | Services: the running containers of those servers, each with the widget that fits its image (linuxserver/radarr gets radarr) and its address: the container’s name when it shares a network with the dashboard, its own address on a macvlan or ipvlan network (Unraid’s br0), or the published port. Tick the ones you want, fill in what the widget needs (a key), and Test shows whether it answers. Next checks every ticked service first: a name, a link (the published address, else the widget’s URL, editable), the widget’s required options, and a test of the widget; one that fails is marked in red with its error, and the wizard stays until it is fixed or unticked. Containers with dashboard.* labels are on the page already and left out. Add a service by hand adds one without a container; Migrate from homepage takes homepage’s services.yaml, settings.yaml, bookmarks.yaml, widgets.yaml and docker.yaml, shows what carries over (and which widgets have no match), and writes them as they are in place of what the wizard would write (services.yaml). | Security: the admin password (required, at least 8 characters; only its hash is written), whether the dashboard shows a login page or asks only for some presses, and the allowed hosts (the name you opened the wizard by, when it is one). All three go into settings.yaml. Skip the setup on the first step leads here too. | Done: it writes settings.yaml, services.yaml, widgets.yaml (the time, the system’s resources and a search box), bookmarks.yaml, docker.yaml and kubernetes.yaml, removes .onboarding and opens the dashboard. It writes nothing when one of those files is there already. | . A key or password you enter is written into services.yaml as it is; to keep it out of the file, put {{DASHBOARD_VAR_NAME}} in its place and set the variable on the container (see Variables). Skip the setup writes the same files with no services. On the local network (a private address, also through a reverse proxy whose visitors are on it) the wizard opens straight away. From anywhere else it asks for the code the dashboard writes in its log at the start (docker logs dashboard). Wrong codes are slowed down. Once the wizard is done, /setup is gone; it never shows for a config folder that has files. To see it again, empty the folder and restart the container.

6.title: YAML in short
6.content: Every file is YAML, a superset of JSON that is easy to read and write. | Indentation matters. Nested keys go two spaces further in than their parent; never use tabs. | key: value, with a space after the colon. A list item starts with - . | Quote strings with special characters, and always API keys and {{DASHBOARD_VAR_...}} values: key: "{{DASHBOARD_VAR_RADARR_KEY}}". | A broken file is reported at the top of the page, with the file and a path into it. An online checker such as YAML Lint helps to find the spot. | .

7.title: Variables
7.content: Any value can contain {{DASHBOARD_VAR_NAME}} (the environment variable DASHBOARD_VAR_NAME) or {{DASHBOARD_FILE_NAME}} (the contents of the file whose path is in DASHBOARD_FILE_NAME, e.g. a Docker secret). homepage’s {{HOMEPAGE_VAR_*}} and {{HOMEPAGE_FILE_*}} work the same, so an existing homepage environment can be reused. Substituted values are treated as secrets: they never reach the browser. Only these forms are filled in. Anything else in double braces, such as {{SHELLY_PASSWORD}}, stays as written and would reach the service as a wrong key or password; the dashboard warns about it at the top of the page, with the form that works ({{DASHBOARD_VAR_SHELLY_PASSWORD}}, with the environment variable DASHBOARD_VAR_SHELLY_PASSWORD).

8.title: Including other files
8.content: A long services.yaml can be split up. !include <file> puts the YAML of another file at that spot, as if it were written there: . # services.yaml - Infrastructure: - Router: href: http://router.lan - Media: !include services/media.yaml # the services of one group - !include services/home-automation.yaml # whole groups . # services/media.yaml: what would otherwise follow "- Media:" - Plex: href: http://plex.lan:32400 icon: plex - Radarr: !include radarr.yaml # relative to this file: services/radarr.yaml . # services/home-automation.yaml: one or more groups, as in services.yaml - Home automation: - Home Assistant: href: http://homeassistant.lan:8123 - Cameras: [] . The rules: . | Where: as the value of a key (- Media: !include ..., widget: !include ...), as an item in a list, or as a whole file. It works in every config file, also widgets.yaml and bookmarks.yaml. | Lists are joined: an include that is a list item and whose file holds a list adds those items in its place. That is how - !include services/home-automation.yaml adds two groups. A file that holds a map (one service, one widget) is added as one item. | Paths are relative to the file with the !include, use /, and must stay inside the config folder. Only .yaml and .yml files can be included. Keep included files out of plugins/. | Nesting: an included file can include others, up to 8 levels deep. A file that ends up including itself is reported. | Variables and secrets: {{DASHBOARD_VAR_*}} and {{DASHBOARD_FILE_*}} work in included files, and their values stay secret, as in the main files. | Reloading: saving an included file reloads the page, also in a subfolder. | Problems never stop the dashboard. A missing file, a path outside the config folder, a YAML error or a loop is shown with the file and path of the !include (services.yaml › [1].Media: !include services/media.yaml: file not found); that spot stays empty and the rest works. A mistake inside the included services is shown with the path in the file that includes it. | On the settings page an included file is a file of its own, edited and saved there; the !include in the main file stays as it is. A save is checked as part of the main file, and secrets in it are hidden by the main file’s rules (a file included under providers: is secret as a whole). | . Files are only read where an !include names them: a media.yaml next to services.yaml does nothing by itself. !include is this dashboard’s own; homepage does not read it.

9.title: Environment variables
9.content: Settings of the container rather than of the page. | Variable | What | . | DASHBOARD_VAR_*, DASHBOARD_FILE_* | Values for {{DASHBOARD_VAR_*}} and {{DASHBOARD_FILE_*}} (see Variables) | . | DASHBOARD_WIDGET_MEMORY_MB, DASHBOARD_WIDGET_ISOLATION | The widget worker (see Widget worker) | . | DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS | Button scripts as root (see Scripts as root) | . | DASHBOARD_WATCH_POLL | Check the config files every so many seconds, for network shares | . | DASHBOARD_CONFIG_DIR | The config folder, when not run from the image | . | LOG_TARGETS | both, stdout or file (with logpath in settings.yaml) | . Settings page . The gear in the footer opens /settings. General has the page’s look (title, language, theme, colour, the header, cards, fonts and icons, the background), its layout, quick launch, the page and app details (description, favicon, app icons and shortcuts) and a few switches and intervals. Security has the login page or only some actions, how long a login and an unlock last, the allowed hosts, the admin password and passkeys. Groups has the layout block: per group its arrangement, columns, tab, icon, title and folding (nested groups too), and the order of the groups with up and down buttons; an entry for a group that no longer exists can be removed there. Widgets has the plugins list: add, change, order and remove packages (a git repository, an npm package or a folder), see what each is pinned to, and install again or update to the newest. It writes them into settings.yaml, keeping your comments and every key it does not show (layout, plugins, providers, …), which it names; the dashboard follows at once. Services is a form: groups, nested groups and services (link, icon, description, the status check and the rest of a service’s keys) and their widgets (a form per widget from its options, with a test button; secret options stay hidden, lists and keys a widget does not declare stay as written), renamed, moved to another group, added and removed; a group or list that comes from an !include is a block with a link to its file, and the services found by discovery are listed (their labels are their source). “Advanced edit” opens the file as text under Advanced. Header widgets is a form too: the widgets in the header, each with the form of its options, added, reordered and removed. Bookmarks is a form as well: groups and bookmarks (link, abbreviation, icon, description). Docker, Kubernetes and Proxmox are forms of their servers, each with a connection test of what is saved, keeping keys they do not show, such as allowVariables; the Proxmox token secret stays hidden. Advanced shows every config file as text: settings.yaml, the other YAML files and the files they include, custom.css and custom.js. A YAML file shows in colour and is checked while you type, as a save would check it: each problem with its line, the line marked in the editor. It also imports homepage’s files (checked first, then all of them or none; the admin password, login and allowed hosts stay). Each text editor can download its text, with hidden values still hidden, with its comments, and the files it includes. A save is checked first: a mistake is shown with its file and path and nothing is written. Secrets written in a file appear as __SECRET_…__ and stay as they were; if the file was changed elsewhere in the meantime, the page says so instead of overwriting it. The previous versions are kept under .history/ in the config folder (the last ten per file), and one can be loaded back into the editor. The section is in the address (/settings#services). Icon fields show a preview and suggest the files in config/icons and the icons already in use. | It opens with the admin password; a login counts, and the browser stays unlocked as after a press (actions.remember). | A new admin password needs the current one, every time; then every other login ends. Set in the container’s environment, it is changed there. | Without an admin password yet (a dashboard set up before the setup wizard), the page asks to set one first, and only on the local network; nothing else is saved before it. | . Allowed hosts . allowedHosts in settings.yaml lists the host names you open the dashboard by. The setup wizard writes it, and the settings page adds and removes names (open the dashboard by its IP address to get there). There is no environment variable for it (DASHBOARD_ALLOWED_HOSTS is no longer read). # settings.yaml allowedHosts: [dash.lan, dash.example.com] # every name you open it by . | Always answered: localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1] (the image’s health check uses them) and any IP address (http://192.168.1.10:3000), with or without the list. | A host name (dash.lan, the name your reverse proxy passes on) is only answered when it is in the list. Otherwise the browser shows a page that says which line to add, with the name it was opened by. An API call gets a 403. A change of settings.yaml counts at once. | Ports: an entry without a port allows every port (dash.lan); with one, only that port (dash.example.com:8443). | * answers every host, as before this check. Only use it when something else checks the host, such as a reverse proxy that answers your names only; the log warns about it. Nothing else can make up for it: to the browser a rebinding page is the dashboard’s own site. | . This stops DNS rebinding: a web page that points a name of its own at your network would otherwise be the same site as the dashboard to your browser, and could read it and press its buttons. Such a page always uses its own name, never an IP address, so IP addresses stay safe. Admin password . The admin password guards what runs something, and with login: true the whole page. It is adminPassword in settings.yaml: only its scrypt hash, never the password itself (a plain one is refused, and what it guards stays locked). The setup wizard writes it, the settings page changes it, and node src/hash-password.mjs in the container asks for a password and prints a new hash: . docker exec -it dashboard node src/hash-password.mjs . # settings.yaml adminPassword: "scrypt:16384:8:1:..." # the printed line . There is no environment variable for it (DASHBOARD_ADMIN_PASSWORD and DASHBOARD_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE are no longer read). Next to the password, a passkey works too. These presses ask for it: . | Buttons that run as root (user: root) ask by default; confirm: none on the entry turns that off. | Other buttons ask when their entry says confirm: password. | target: hidden-iframe services (a webhook the dashboard calls) ask; confirm: none on the service turns that off. | The widget sync (POST /api/plugins/sync) asks too. | . confirm: always asks on every press. Otherwise a correct password unlocks that browser for 15 minutes (actions: { remember: 30m } in settings.yaml, 0 asks every time); the lock in the footer locks it again, and a restart of the dashboard locks every browser. # services.yaml - Admin: - Update: widgets: - type: button text: Update containers command: docker compose -f /stack/compose.yaml up -d --pull always confirm: password # ask, then remember for 15 minutes - type: button text: Reboot user: root # asks by default command: reboot confirm: always # every press . The dialog has a username (dashboard) and a password field, so a password manager or the browser’s own keychain (with Face ID or Touch ID) fills it in. | Scripts inside the container (a button’s curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/...) are not asked: a request from 127.0.0.1 without a proxy header comes from the container itself. A reverse proxy on the same machine with host networking must send X-Forwarded-For (they all do by default), or its visitors count as the container too. | Guessing is slowed down: after five wrong passwords from one address it waits 30 seconds, doubled each time (up to 15 minutes). Each wrong one is in the log. | Open the dashboard over HTTPS when it asks for a password: over plain HTTP the password crosses the network as it is. | Labels of a discovered container cannot set confirm: none. | . Login page . With login: true in settings.yaml the page itself asks for the admin password: whoever opens the dashboard sees a login page first, and every API call without a session gets a . | Logged in counts as unlocked: buttons ask nothing more, except those with confirm: always. The logout is in the footer. | . # settings.yaml login: true # or { remember: 30d } . | A session lasts a week (remember) and each visit moves its end on: a dashboard you open every day keeps you logged in. A week without a visit ends it. | Sessions live on the server, in .sessions.json in the config folder (hashes of the tokens only, readable by the dashboard alone): the server checks every request, they last through a restart or an update, a logout ends one for good (also if its cookie was copied), and a new admin password ends them all. | The cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (Secure over HTTPS): a link to the dashboard from elsewhere opens it logged in, while the endpoints that change something keep needing a header no other site can send. | Still open: /api/health (the image’s health check) and robots.txt; and, as for the presses, scripts inside the container. | Without an admin password, login: true does nothing but say so in the messages. | . Passkeys . Next to the admin password, a passkey (your fingerprint, face or a PIN, on this device or your phone) works wherever the dashboard asks for authentication: the login page, the settings and the buttons. Add one on the settings page, under Passkeys. Where one can be used, the dashboard asks for it at once; cancel it to type the admin password, which keeps working. A new password leaves the passkeys as they are. | Over HTTPS, by a host name only. Browsers offer passkeys in a secure context only, and a passkey belongs to the host name it was added on: one made on https://dash.example.com works there, not on https://dash.lan or an IP address. Behind a reverse proxy, the proxy passes X-Forwarded-Proto: https and keeps the Host header (most do by default). | Stored in .passkeys.json in the config folder: the public keys only, readable by the dashboard alone. Remove a passkey on the settings page; deleting the file removes them all. | The passkey has to verify you (user verification), and wrong tries are slowed down as for the password. | . Authentication in front . The login page closes the dashboard with one password (and passkeys). For accounts of your own, single sign-on or a second factor, put an authenticating proxy in front instead, or as well: Authelia, Authentik, Cloudflare Access, oauth2-proxy. The dashboard needs nothing for it; it sees only requests the proxy let through. # compose.yaml: Traefik with Authelia's forward auth services: dashboard: image: ghcr.io/stefanrenne/dashboard:latest volumes: [./config:/config] # no ports: only the proxy reaches it labels: - traefik.http.routers.dashboard.rule=Host(`dash.example.com`) - traefik.http.routers.dashboard.middlewares=authelia@docker # the forwardAuth middleware from Authelia's own labels - traefik.http.services.dashboard.loadbalancer.server.port=3000 . # Caddyfile: the same with Caddy dash.example.com { forward_auth authelia:9091 { uri /api/authz/forward-auth copy_headers Remote-User Remote-Groups Remote-Email Remote-Name } reverse_proxy dashboard:3000 } . Authentik’s proxy outpost works the same (its forward-auth middleware in Traefik, or forward_auth to the outpost in Caddy). With Cloudflare Access, add an Access application for the host name and let the tunnel point at http://dashboard:3000. | Publish no port of the dashboard (no ports:), or bind it to 127.0.0.1: the dashboard always answers IP addresses, so http://<server>:3000 would go around the proxy. | Add the host name to Allowed hosts. | Leave everything behind the proxy, /api/health included: the image’s health check calls it inside the container, not through the proxy. | /api/events is a stream that stays open: a proxy that buffers responses (nginx: proxy_buffering off; for it) delays the page’s reloads otherwise. | Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy’s address, so wrong admin passwords are slowed down for everyone at once. Keep the admin password for the buttons anyway: the proxy decides who sees the page, the password who presses user: root. | . Widget worker . Installed widgets run in a worker thread with a memory limit, so one that hangs cannot stop the dashboard. DASHBOARD_WIDGET_MEMORY_MB sets the limit (default 256); DASHBOARD_WIDGET_ISOLATION=off runs them in the dashboard process instead. The worker’s environment leaves out the DASHBOARD_VAR_* and DASHBOARD_FILE_* variables (and HOMEPAGE_): a widget gets the values the config gives it, through its options, not every one. Scripts as root . The button widget runs its script as the dashboard’s user (node, uid 1000). A button with user: root runs it as root inside the container, for scripts that write files owned by root. That only works with DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS: "true" on the container: the image then lets node start one fixed runner (/usr/local/bin/dashboard-root) through sudo. Without it such a button shows that it needs the variable. The container must start as root (the default; not --user 1000), since that is when the rule is written. Every installed widget could use the runner once it is on, and anyone who can open the page can press the button, so turn it on only for a dashboard you trust and keep behind authentication. # docker-compose.yml services: dashboard: environment: DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS: "true" .

11.title: Custom widget
11.content: Every widget on the dashboard is a package: a folder with a widget.yaml and usually a server.js. Even the widgets behind the dashboard’s own service fields (siteMonitor:, container:, …) come from the widgets collection this way, so anything they do, a widget of yours can do too. Nobody has to merge a pull request here first. my-widget/ widget.yaml the manifest: id, name, apiVersion, options server.js fetch(ctx): asks your service, returns blocks client.js optional: a Web Component for a look of its own i18n.json optional: labels in the dashboard's languages . A widget is written the same way wherever it lives; only how the dashboard gets it differs. Both are listed under plugins: in settings.yaml. |   | Where | For | . | Local widget | A folder next to your config, path: ./my-widgets/x | Something only you need, or trying out a widget while you write it. Start here: it walks through writing one. | . | Remote widget | A git repository or an npm package, source: git+https://...#v1.0.0 | Sharing it: others install it with one line, pinned to a version, and it can be listed in the Catalogue. | . The API reference has every field of widget.yaml, ctx and the result; Security what a widget can reach.

Nobody has to merge a pull request here first. | Page | What | . | Custom widget | Writing a widget: as a local folder, or as a remote package others install | . | API reference | widget.yaml, the ctx passed to server.js, the result format, client.js | . | Security | What a widget can do, how secrets stay on the server, advice for users | . | Contributing | Working on the dashboard itself | .

17.title: Your whole homelab on one page
17.content: A fast, self-hosted start page for your homelab. Write a few lines of YAML and every service gets a card with its live numbers: the queue of Radarr, the VMs on Proxmox, the blocked queries of Pi-hole, the photos in Immich. And when a widget for your service does not exist yet, you can publish one yourself, from your own repository, without waiting for anyone. Get started Browse the widgets .

18.title: Why you will like it
18.content: 180+ widgets, ready to go. Radarr, Sonarr, Plex, Jellyfin, Proxmox, Unraid, TrueNAS, Pi-hole, AdGuard, Home Assistant, Immich, Portainer, UniFi, Traefik and many more, plus the weather, stocks and a generic JSON mapper for anything with an API. They are installed with the dashboard and keep themselves up to date. See them all. Widgets anyone can publish. Every widget is a small package: a manifest and one function. Put it in a git repository or on npm, and others add it with one line of YAML. No pull request to get merged, no release to wait for. Write your own. Configured in YAML, live on save. Services, header widgets, bookmarks: plain files you can keep in git. Save one and every open page updates by itself. A mistake is shown on the page, with the file and the spot in it, and the rest keeps working. Configuration. Finds your services by itself. Label a Docker container or annotate a Kubernetes Ingress and it appears on the page, with its status. Docker Swarm, Traefik IngressRoutes and the Gateway API too. Docker · Kubernetes. Buttons for the jobs you repeat. Pull new images, pause downloads, start a backup, reboot a node: a button on a card runs a script or command on the server, and shows the output when it fails. Button widget. Your keys stay on your server. API keys and passwords go in variables and never reach the browser; widgets run in a worker with a timeout, so one broken service never takes the page down. Security. Feels at home. Coming from homepage? Its services.yaml, widgets.yaml, Docker labels and {{HOMEPAGE_VAR_*}} variables work as they are (see From homepage). Dark and light themes, 22 accent colours, tabs, 17 languages, and it installs as an app on your phone.

19.title: Get started in a minute
19.content: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -v ./config:/config ghcr.io/stefanrenne/dashboard:latest . Open http://localhost:3000. On a first start, with an empty config folder, a setup wizard opens: pick a title, language and colour, tick the running containers you want on the page (it recognises them and fills in their widget and address), bring your homepage files along if you have them, and check the security settings. It writes the YAML files and steps aside (see First start). From then on, edit services.yaml and watch the page follow: . # services.yaml - Media: - Radarr: href: http://radarr.lan icon: radarr.svg siteMonitor: http://radarr.lan widget: type: radarr url: http://radarr.lan:7878 key: "{{DASHBOARD_VAR_RADARR_KEY}}" . With Docker Compose # compose.yaml services: dashboard: image: ghcr.io/stefanrenne/dashboard:latest ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - ./config:/config - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro # optional: Docker status and discovery; :ro does not limit the API, see Docker environment: DASHBOARD_VAR_RADARR_KEY: your-api-key restart: unless-stopped . To open the dashboard by a name, add it under Allowed hosts on the settings page. For Docker discovery through a read-only socket proxy, see Docker. Images are built for amd64 and arm64 for every release: latest is the newest release, and each has its own tag (0.14.0, 0.14). What changed in each release is in the CHANGELOG.

22.title: AdGuard Home
22.content: type: adguard · version 0.3.2 · widget API 2 · Widget collection develop · source . DNS queries, queries blocked by the filter lists, queries filtered by Safe Browsing, Safe Search and parental control, and the average processing time, as homepage’s adguard widget. Over the statistics period set in AdGuard Home (Settings > General settings > Statistics). username and password are the login of AdGuard Home’s web interface. Learn more about AdGuard Home.

23.title: Display fields
23.content: queries, blocked, filtered, latency . Pick them with fields: in the entry.

24.title: Configuration options
24.content: | Option | Type | Required | Default | Description | . | url | url | yes |   | E.g. http://adguard.lan:3000 | . | username | string |   |   | The web interface login | . | password | string |   |   | Secret: stays on the server. | . Every widget also takes refresh (or refreshInterval in ms), fields and hideErrors; see Services.

25.title: Filter attributes
25.content: Public values a service’s filter: can read, as widget.<attribute>; see Filters. | Attribute | Type | Description | . | queries | number | DNS queries answered | . | blocked | number | DNS queries blocked by the filter lists | . | filtered | number | Queries replaced by Safe Browsing, Safe Search or parental control | . | latency | number | Average processing time of a query, in ms | .

26.title: Example
26.content: # services.yaml - Network: - AdGuard Home: href: http://adguard.lan:3000 icon: adguard-home widget: type: adguard fields: [queries, blocked, filtered, latency] # the display fields; leave out for the defaults url: http://adguard.lan:3000 username: admin password: "{{DASHBOARD_VAR_ADGUARD_PASSWORD}}" .

28.title: APC UPS
28.content: type: apcups · version 0.4.0 · widget API 2 · Widget collection develop · source . Status (on battery and a lost connection marked), load, battery charge and runtime left of an APC UPS, read from apcupsd’s network information server, as homepage’s apcups widget. apcupsd listens on 127.0.0.1 by default: set NISIP in /etc/apcupsd.conf to an address the dashboard can reach (and keep NETSERVER on), then restart apcupsd. url is that address and port, tcp://host:3551. Learn more about apcupsd.

29.title: Display fields
29.content: status, load, bcharge, timeleft . Pick them with fields: in the entry.

30.title: Configuration options
30.content: | Option | Type | Required | Default | Description | . | url | string | yes |   | Apcupsd’s network server, e.g. tcp://nas.lan:3551 | . Every widget also takes refresh (or refreshInterval in ms), fields and hideErrors; see Services.

31.title: Filter attributes
31.content: Public values a service’s filter: can read, as widget.<attribute>; see Filters. | Attribute | Type | Description | . | status | string | The UPS’s state: online, onBattery or lost | . | load | number | Load on the UPS, in % of its capacity | . | bcharge | number | Battery charge, in % | . | timeleft | number | Minutes the battery lasts at the current load | . | attention | boolean | True while the card marks something as needing attention | .

32.title: Example
32.content: # services.yaml - Infrastructure: - UPS: icon: apc widget: type: apcups fields: [status, load, bcharge, timeleft] # the display fields; leave out for the defaults url: tcp://nas.lan:3551 .

34.title: Widget API reference
34.content: This is the contract between the dashboard and widget packages (hard rule 2 in CLAUDE.md). Current widget API: 1. Every addition is listed with the version that introduced it.

35.title: Package layout
35.content: my-widget/ widget.yaml required manifest server.js optional data on the server client.js optional custom rendering in the browser i18n.json optional translations assets/ optional static files for client.js, served at /widgets/<id>/assets/... package.json optional only for npm publishing; must contain "type": "module" . Load assets relative to your module, not from an absolute path, so the widget also works when the dashboard runs under a sub path (base in settings.yaml): new URL('./assets/icon.svg', import.meta.url). A package without server.js is client-only (like datetime and search). A package without client.js is rendered by the dashboard from blocks.

36.title: widget.yaml
36.content: | Key | Required | Meaning | . | id | yes | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes, max 63. Used as type: in the config and as dash-<id> element name. | . | name | yes | Human-readable name. | . | version | yes | A string, e.g. "1.2.0". Installed as plugins/<id>@<version>. | . | apiVersion | yes | The widget API this package targets: 2. A widget of API 1 is not loaded; see API 1. | . | description | no | One line, for docs and catalogues. | . | refresh | no | Cache time of a result: 500ms, 10s, 5m, 1h or seconds. Default 30s. The browser polls at this rate (minimum 2 s). | . | options | no | Map of option name to schema (below). | . | aliases | no | Other names the widget answers to in type:, e.g. homepage’s ([customapi]). Added after every real id, only where still free; the widget’s id stays the one the page uses. | . | defaultFields | no | Block keys shown when the entry has no fields, e.g. [cpu, memoryPercent]. Without it every block shows. | . | images | no | Docker images the setup wizard of a first install recognises the service by, when the image’s name is not the widget’s id or one of its aliases, e.g. [plexinc/pms-docker] (a repository without registry and tag, or only its last part). | . | confirmWhen | no | Option values for which a press of the widget’s action asks for the admin password by default, e.g. { user: root }. An entry’s confirm: (password, always, none) overrides it. Only counts when the dashboard has an admin password. | . | frames | no | url options whose page the client.js shows in an <iframe>, e.g. [src]. The page’s CSP allows the origin of each one’s value (frame-src); only public options count, so a URL from a variable or a secret option is never framed. | . | attributes | no | Public values the widget publishes for a service’s filter:, each name: { type: <type>, from? } with boolean, number or string. A line comment says what it means; the docs page lists them. See Filter attributes. | . | params | no | Names a client.js may send its server.js through the dash-widget-params page event, e.g. [latitude, longitude]. They reach ctx.params; anything else is dropped. | . Filter attributes . Users hide a service’s card with filter: on these values, e.g. filter: widget.queued == 0. Each one either comes from the result the widget already returns, named with from:, or is returned by fetch in attributes: . attributes: queued: { type: number, from: queued } # the value of the `queued` block attention: { type: boolean, from: '@attention' } # true when a block or row is marked warn or error status: { type: string, from: '@status' } # the result's status: up, down, ... streams: { type: number, from: '@rows' } # the number of rows (a "+3 more" row counts 3) vmsStopped: { type: number } # no from: fetch returns it in attributes . from: <block key> takes the block’s value before fields: picks the blocks, and null when the widget left the block out. Use it for blocks whose value is a plain number or state; a value formatted for the card (“1.2 TB”, “2d 4h”) makes a poor filter, so return the raw number in attributes instead. What fetch returns in attributes wins over from:. Option schema . | Key | Meaning | . | type | string (a number or boolean becomes text), url (http/https only), number, boolean, list (a comma string is split), object, enum, icon (see below) | . | values | For enum: the allowed values. | . | required | true makes a missing option an error on the card and in the config messages. | . | default | Used when the option is missing. | . | secret | true keeps the option on the server. | . | discoverable | false: the option is only taken from the YAML config, never from a Docker label or Kubernetes annotation (whoever starts a container writes those). For options that run something or reach elsewhere with the dashboard’s rights, such as the button’s command. Options listed in frames are never taken from a label either. | . An icon option takes what a service’s icon: takes (plex.svg, mdi-home, si-ubuntu, sh-plex, /icons/x.png, a URL) and reaches the widget as a URL. A single-colour icon (mdi-, si-) ends in #dash-mask, or #dash-mask=<hex> with its colour: draw it as a CSS mask over the URL before the #, filled with that colour or a theme colour. An unknown name is an error. What reaches the browser: only options that are declared, not secret, and not filled in from a variable or file. Undeclared options are passed to server.js but never to the browser.

37.title: server.js
37.content: export default { async fetch(ctx) { return { blocks: [{ label: 'queries', value: 1234 }] }; }, }; . fetch(ctx) is called at most once per refresh per widget instance. Concurrent browser requests share one call. action . export default { async fetch(ctx) { return { blocks: [] }; }, async action(ctx) { return { status: 'ok', output: 'done', exitCode: 0 }; }, }; . Optional. Runs when the widget’s client.js sends dash-widget-action (a button press): the page POSTs api/widgets/<instanceId>/action and shows the result in a dialog. Same ctx as fetch; ctx.signal aborts after an hour at most (keep your own, shorter limit). One action at a time per instance: a second press while one runs is refused. With an admin password on the dashboard, the page first asks for it when the entry or widget.yaml confirmWhen says so. Afterwards the other widgets and status labels on the same card ask again, dimmed until they answer: right away, and after 5 and 30 seconds for services that take a moment to notice (the server keeps their results 4 seconds meanwhile). So a button that updates containers, next to a widget that counts updates, shows the new count. The result: . | Field | Meaning | . | status | ok, or anything else for a failure. | . | output | Text shown as it is (monospace, scrollable); the last 64 KB are kept. | . | exitCode | An integer, shown next to the status. | . | error | A short reason for a failure. | . Other fields are dropped. Every secret value the dashboard knows (secret options, {{DASHBOARD_VAR_*}}, {{DASHBOARD_FILE_*}}) is replaced by *** in output and error, as is a thrown error’s message. An action changes something somewhere: it runs for anyone who can open the page (there is no login), so say so in the widget’s README. Widgets run in a worker thread, apart from the dashboard: one worker for all of them, with a memory limit. ctx is the same; what fetch returns must be plain data (it is copied out of the worker), and module-level state is the worker’s. A widget that does not stop within a second after its timeout gets the worker restarted. ctx . | Field | Meaning | . | ctx.apiVersion | the widget’s apiVersion: 2 | . | ctx.instanceId | Stable id of this instance (group + service + position). | . | ctx.options | Validated options, secrets included. A copy: changing it has no effect. | . | ctx.fetch(url, init) | The standard fetch, plus: relative URLs resolve against options.url; the call is aborted with the widget; init.socketPath sends the request over a unix socket (used for Docker); init.insecure: true accepts a self-signed certificate for that request (only behind an option the user sets, off by default); init.tls: { ca, cert, key } (PEM text) trusts that CA and sends that client certificate, as for a Docker daemon with --tlsverify. res.headers.getSetCookie() lists every cookie. | . | ctx.params | What the page sent through dash-widget-params: only names in widget.yaml params, each a non-empty string of at most 100 characters; {} when nothing was sent. Comes from the browser, so treat it as untrusted input (validate, never put it in a URL path unchecked). Each set of params has its own cached result; at most 30 sets a minute per instance call the widget afresh (more get an error), so round values in client.js (coordinates to two decimals) and validate them in server.js. | . | ctx.signal | AbortSignal, aborted when the call times out (10 s). | . | ctx.cache | A Map that survives between calls of this instance (e.g. the previous value for a delta). Cleared when the instance disappears from the config, and when the widget worker restarts (see below). | . | ctx.configDir | The dashboard’s config folder (an absolute path), e.g. to resolve a script path from the options. | . | ctx.log | info, warn, error; prefixed with the widget type. | . Only node: built-ins can be imported. Bundle any other dependency into the file. Result . An object; all fields are optional. | Field | Meaning | . | status | up, down, warn or unknown. Used when the widget is a service’s status check. | . | latency | Milliseconds, shown next to the status dot. | . | statusText | Text for the status label in the card corner instead of the latency (e.g. healthy). Translated when it is a key. | . | blocks | List of { key?, label, vars?, value, unit?, status? }. label is a string, translated through i18n.json when it is a key; vars fill {name} placeholders in that translation ({ label: 'poolUsed', vars: { pool: 'Trunk' } } with "poolUsed": "{pool} used"). value is a string, number or null (shown as –). A string value is translated too when it is a key. status is ok, warn, error or unknown: warn and error get a colour and a shape (▲, ✕) and are announced to screen readers. key names the block for fields (default: the label). | . | attributes | Map of the attributes declared in widget.yaml to their value (of the declared type, or null): { update: true, version: '1.4.2' }. Users filter services on them (filter: widget.update == false). They are public: they reach the browser, so never put a secret in one (a secret value is replaced by ***). Undeclared names and values of another type are left out, with one warning in the log. fields and highlight do not touch them. | . | rows | List of { label, vars?, value?, status?, icon?, progress? }, shown below the blocks as label-left/value-right lines (a download queue, current streams, display: list). status marks a row like a block. icon (play or pause) is drawn before the label and spoken as a word. progress (0–100) fills the row’s background. A row whose text does not fit opens on click, Enter or Space. A row labelled moreItems with vars: { count } closes a shortened list (“+3 more”). | . Writing labels . Labels sit in blocks of about 65px on a phone when a card has four of them. Keep every translation short: whole words (no abbreviations), at most two lines; the dashboard wraps and hyphenates in the page language, and never cuts a label off. Show amounts in decimal units (kB, MB, GB) and durations as m:ss or h:mm:ss. Mark counts that need someone’s attention (failures, pending requests, updates) with status: 'warn'. | anything else | Free-form JSON for client.js. | . Keys the dashboard keeps for itself . These keys in a widget entry are read by the dashboard and not passed to the widget, unless the widget declares an option with the same name: . | Key | Meaning | . | refreshInterval | Refresh time of this instance in milliseconds (homepage’s name). Minimum 1000. | . | refresh | The same as a duration: 5s, 1h. A bare number of 1000 or more is milliseconds (homepage’s refresh: 3000); a smaller one is seconds. | . | fields | List of block keys to show, e.g. [cpu, memoryPercent]. The widget’s order is kept. | . | hideErrors / hide_errors | true hides the error box of this widget. | . | provider | Fills options the entry leaves out from settings.yaml providers.<name>: a map fills the options it names, a text the first unset secret: true option. Every provider value is treated as a secret. A widget that declares its own provider option keeps it. | . | highlight | Colours blocks by their value, as in homepage: block key (or <type>.<key>) → numeric / string rules with a level (good, warn, danger). The dashboard adds the result to the block as highlight: { level, valueOnly }; client.js sees it in data.blocks and may use or ignore it. See Services. | . References to another service (homepage’s calendar integrations): an object anywhere in a widget’s options (up to three levels deep) with service_group and service_name gets that service’s widget options (with type, the widget of that type) under its own keys, on the server. Declare the option secret: true (or leave it undeclared): the merged options can hold keys. An unknown service is a config message. A thrown error (or a timeout) shows its message on the card. Secret values in it are replaced by ***.

38.title: client.js
38.content: A JavaScript module that defines a custom element named dash-<id>: . class MyWidget extends HTMLElement { connectedCallback() { this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }); this.render(); } set data(v) { this._data = v; this.render(); } render() { /* ... */ } } customElements.define('dash-my-widget', MyWidget); . The dashboard sets these properties before the element is connected, and data and error again after every refresh: . | Property | Meaning | . | options | Public options only. | . | t(key) | Translation from i18n.json for the dashboard language, falling back to English, then the key. | . | data | What server.js returned, or null (before the first result, or for a client-only widget). | . | error | Error message of the last refresh, or null. | . | instanceId | The id of this widget instance (for api/suggest). | . | busy | true while an action this widget asked for (dash-widget-action) runs, then false. Use a setter to update the look (disable the button). | . | actionResult | { status: 'ok' } or { status: 'error' } of the last action, set just before busy goes back to false, e.g. to show a check after a quiet success. | . Theme CSS variables inherit into the shadow root: --dash-text, --dash-muted, --dash-accent, --dash-card, --dash-border, --dash-ok, --dash-warn, --dash-error. API 1 . The dashboard no longer loads a widget with apiVersion: 1; the configuration messages name it. API 2 renamed the page’s names and changed nothing else, so moving a widget over is renaming: set apiVersion: 2, and in its client.js the element hd-<id> becomes dash-<id>, the events hd-widget-action, hd-widget-params, hd-search-input and hd-search-submit become dash-…, the theme properties --hd-* become --dash-* and the icon marker #hd-mask becomes #dash-mask. The page’s Content-Security-Policy allows connect-src 'self': get data through server.js, not from the browser. Images may come from anywhere.

39.title: Page events
39.content: A client.js may talk to the dashboard through DOM events that bubble out of its shadow root (bubbles: true, composed: true): . | Event | detail | What the dashboard does | . | dash-search-input | { query } | Shows only the services and bookmarks that match every word; empty shows all. | . | dash-search-submit | { query } | Send it cancelable: true. With exactly one match the dashboard opens it and cancels the event; otherwise the widget may search elsewhere. | . | dash-widget-action | { title?, showResult? } | Runs server.js’s action (see above) and shows its result in a dialog titled title (default: the service’s name). Sets the element’s busy to true until it is done and then its actionResult; a press while it runs is ignored. showResult: 'failure' is for a widget that shows its own progress: no running toast, and the dialog only when the action failed. | . | dash-widget-params | { name: value, ... } | Fetches the widget again with these values (text) for server.js, and keeps sending them on every refresh. Only the names in widget.yaml params arrive. | . The collection’s search widget uses the first two. The weather widgets of the collection send dash-widget-params with the viewer’s location (navigator.geolocation, HTTPS only, rounded to two decimals) when their options have no coordinates.

40.title: Dashboard endpoints for client.js
40.content: | Request | Answer | . | GET api/suggest?instance=<instanceId>&q=<text> | { suggestions: [...] }: search suggestions for this instance, when its options have showSearchSuggestions: true and a provider (google, duckduckgo, bing, baidu, brave) or provider: custom with a suggestionUrl. The server asks the search engine; the URL never comes from the request. Empty on any problem. | . Use relative URLs (api/...), so the widget also works under a sub path.

41.title: i18n.json
41.content: { "en": { "queries": "Queries" }, "nl": { "queries": "Verzoeken" } } . Languages: en, nl, fr, de, es. Missing keys fall back to English, then the key itself.

42.title: Changes
42.content: | API | Dashboard | Change | . | 2 | next | discoverable: false on an option: not taken from a discovered service. Discovered services also lose frames options, provider and service_group/service_name. Older dashboards ignore the key. | . | 2 | next | images in widget.yaml, for the setup wizard. Widgets need no change. | . | 2 | next | With login: true every endpoint (also GET api/widgets/<instanceId>) answers 401 { needsLogin: true } without a session; the page goes to its login. Widgets need no change. | . | 2 | next | confirmWhen in widget.yaml, and the admin password: POST api/widgets/<instanceId>/action answers 401 { needsPassword: true } (or 429 with retryAfter) until it has one; the page asks for it. Widgets need no change. | . | 2 | next | API 1 is no longer supported: such a widget is not loaded, with a message that says what to rename. | . | 2 | next | The names of the page: the element dash-<id>, the events dash-widget-action, dash-widget-params, dash-search-input and dash-search-submit, the theme properties --dash-* and the icon marker #dash-mask. Nothing else changed: a widget of API 1 goes to 2 by renaming them. | . | 1 | 0.1.0 | First version (including vars, row status and defaultFields). | . | 1 | 0.8.0 | action(ctx) in server.js, ctx.configDir, the hd-widget-action event and the element’s busy; POST api/widgets/<instanceId>/action. | . | 1 | 0.10.0 | showResult: 'failure' in hd-widget-action, and the element’s actionResult. | . | 1 | next | attributes in widget.yaml and in the result: public values a service’s filter: reads. Older dashboards ignore them. | . | 1 | next | from: in an attribute: a block key, @attention, @status or @rows. | . | 1 | next | Blocks can carry highlight: { level, valueOnly }, added by the dashboard from the entry’s highlight: rules. Widgets need no change. | . | 1 | next | provider: <name> in an entry fills options from settings.yaml providers. Widgets need no change. | . | 1 | next | client.js gets instanceId; GET api/suggest for search suggestions. | . | 1 | next | Option type icon; string options accept numbers and booleans. | . | 1 | next | aliases in widget.yaml. | . | 1 | next | ctx.fetch(url, { insecure: true }) for self-signed certificates. | . | 1 | next | ctx.fetch(url, { tls: { ca, cert, key } }) for a CA and client certificate. | . | 1 | next | Options with service_group and service_name get the referenced widget’s options. | . | 1 | next | params in widget.yaml, the hd-widget-params page event and ctx.params. | . | 1 | next | frames in widget.yaml: the page may frame the origin of these options. | . | 1 | next | Installed widgets run in a worker thread; their result must be plain data. Widgets that return plain data need no change. | .

50.title: Architecture
50.content: settings.yaml ─┐ services.yaml ─┤ loadConfig ──► config ──┬─► syncPlugins ──► installed dirs ─┐ widgets / bookmarks / … ┘ (+ variables) │ ▼ │ loadRegistry (plugins) ├─► Discovery (Docker, K8s) ──┐ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ mergeDiscovered ──────────────► buildState │ │ instances (full options) layout (public) ▼ ▼ WidgetRuntime ◄── /api/widgets/:id /api/layout ──► index.html . | Reload (app.reload): on start, on a YAML change (fs.watch, debounced) and on POST /api/plugins/sync. Reloads are queued, never interleaved. After a reload the server sends event: reload on /api/events (SSE) and open pages fetch the layout again. | Discovery polls on its own interval and calls rebuild() only when its result changed. | Instances: each service widget, each status check (siteMonitor/ping/container map to the http-status/ping/docker widgets) and each header widget gets a stable id from group/service/position. The runtime caches each instance’s result for its refresh. | Layout: what the browser gets. Public options, resolved icon URLs, per widget type the client.js URL and the strings for the configured language, and config messages. | .

51.title: HTTP
51.content: | Route | What | . | GET / | public/index.html | . | GET /api/layout | Layout JSON | . | GET /api/widgets/:instanceId | { ok, data, fetchedAt } or { ok: false, error } | . | GET /api/events | Server-sent events: reload | . | GET /api/health | { ok, version } (Docker healthcheck) | . | POST /api/plugins/sync[?update=1] | Re-sync plugins; needs X-Requested-With: dashboard | . | POST /api/widgets/:instanceId/action | Runs the widget’s action; { ok, data: { status, output?, exitCode?, error? } }, { ok: false, error }, 409 while one runs, 404 without an action. Same header. | . | POST /api/run/:serviceId | Calls the configured URL of a target: hidden-iframe service; { ok, status } or { ok: false, error }. Same header. | . | GET /widgets/:type/client.js, /widgets/:type/assets/* | Widget browser files | . | GET /icons/* | <config>/icons | . HEAD is answered like GET.

121.title: Button
121.content: type: button · version 1.5.2 · widget API 2 · Widget collection develop · source . A button on a card or in the header that opens a link, or runs a script or a shell command on the dashboard’s server, for jobs such as pulling new images, restarting a stack or starting a backup. Set exactly one of href, script or command; with none or several, the card shows an error. | href opens the page in a new tab. | script runs a file with bash. A relative path is relative to the config folder (/config in the container), which is also the folder the run starts in. | command runs a line with bash -c, such as docker compose -f stacks/media.yaml pull. | . While it runs, the button shows a spinner instead of its label and cannot be pressed. A run that succeeds (exit code 0) shows a check for a moment, then the label again. A run that fails opens the dashboard’s result dialog with the output (stdout and stderr together, the last 64 kB) and the exit code; the output can be copied from there. A run that takes longer than timeout seconds (default 300) is stopped, together with everything it started. Values filled in from {{DASHBOARD_VAR_*}} are scrubbed from the output. The run gets only PATH and HOME from the dashboard’s environment; set inheritEnv: true to pass all of it, except the DASHBOARD_VAR_* and DASHBOARD_FILE_* variables when the button runs in the dashboard’s widget worker (the default). Give a script a value in its command instead: command: TOKEN={{DASHBOARD_VAR_TOKEN}} scripts/deploy.sh. It runs as the dashboard’s user (node, uid 1000, in the image), so tools such as curl, jq or docker must be in the image and the Docker socket must allow that user. Running as root . user: root runs the script as root inside the container, for a script that writes files which must stay owned by root (a proxy’s config, chown). It needs DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS: "true" in the dashboard container’s environment; without it the button says so. The dashboard itself keeps running as node: the image lets it start one fixed runner as root through sudo, and only when that variable is set. HOME is then /root; inheritEnv: true passes the dashboard’s environment to the root script too. A timeout stops the root script and what it started. Once the variable is on, any installed widget could run as root in the container, so set it only on a dashboard you trust. Anyone who can open the dashboard can press the button: put the dashboard behind authentication before you add buttons that change things. script and command are kept on the server; the browser only gets the label. script, command, user and inheritEnv are only taken from services.yaml: a button found through Docker labels or Kubernetes annotations can open a link, but runs nothing (the dashboard names the label in its messages). Labels are written by whoever starts a container, or come with its image. Asking for a password . With an admin password on the dashboard (adminPassword in its settings.yaml, which its setup wizard and settings page write), a press can ask for that password first. A button with user: root asks by default; any button asks with confirm: password (then that browser stays unlocked for a while, 15 minutes by default) or confirm: always (every press). confirm: none turns it off for a root button. Without an admin password nothing asks, and the dashboard’s messages name the buttons that would. See the dashboard’s Admin password. With the dashboard’s login page (login: true) a login counts: only confirm: always asks again. Several buttons on one card are several button widgets, each one full width.

122.title: Display fields
122.content: No blocks: the button is drawn by the widget.

123.title: Configuration options
123.content: | Option | Type | Required | Default | Description | . | text | string | yes |   | The button’s label | . | href | url |   |   | Opens this page in a new tab, e.g. https://grafana.lan/ | . | script | string |   |   | Secret: stays on the server. A bash script to run, e.g. scripts/update.sh (relative to the config folder) | . | command | string |   |   | Secret: stays on the server. A shell command to run with bash -c, e.g. docker compose pull | . | timeout | number |   | 300 | Seconds before the run is stopped | . | inheritEnv | boolean |   | false | Give the run the dashboard’s environment (without DASHBOARD_VAR_*), not only PATH and HOME | . | user | node / root |   | node | Root needs DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS=true on the dashboard container | . Every widget also takes refresh (or refreshInterval in ms), fields and hideErrors; see Services.

124.title: Filter attributes
124.content: Public values a service’s filter: can read, as widget.<attribute>; see Filters. | Attribute | Type | Description | . | attention | boolean | True while the card marks something as needing attention | .

125.title: Example
125.content: # services.yaml - Media: - Jellyfin: href: https://jellyfin.lan widgets: - type: button text: Pull new images command: docker compose -f stacks/media.yaml pull timeout: 600 confirm: password # with an admin password: ask first - type: button text: Back up the library script: scripts/backup-jellyfin.sh - type: button text: Release notes href: https://github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin/releases - Proxy: - SWAG: widget: type: button text: Generate proxy configs command: cd /srv/configs && ./gen-swag.sh user: root # needs DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS: "true" on the dashboard container .

133.title: Calendar
133.content: type: calendar · version 0.3.0 · widget API 2 · Widget collection develop · source . A month with a coloured dot per event and the chosen day’s events below it, or with view: agenda a list of the coming events, as homepage’s calendar widget. Events come from integrations: Sonarr (episodes), Radarr (cinema, physical and digital releases), Lidarr (albums) and Readarr (books), and any iCal feed (Google Calendar, Nextcloud, …). Use the arrows to page through months; done items (a file is there) are dimmed, and items link to baseUrl when it is set. An integration of an *arr points to a service on the dashboard with service_group and service_name, as in homepage: the dashboard fills in that widget’s url and key on the server. Or give url and key yourself. params: { unmonitored: true } also shows unmonitored items. An iCal integration takes the feed’s url and a name (params: { showName: true } puts it before each title); for Google Calendar use Settings > your calendar > Integrate calendar > Secret address in iCal format. Repeating events are expanded (daily, weekly with days, monthly, yearly; with INTERVAL, COUNT, UNTIL and EXDATE). timezone sets the zone the days are counted in (default the viewer’s). showTime: true shows the time of today’s events. Learn more about iCalendar.

188.title: Custom CSS & JS
188.content: The settings page edits both files under Advanced; the previous versions are kept there too. A custom.css and a custom.js in the config folder are loaded after the page’s own style and script, as in homepage. Refresh the browser after a change: unlike the YAML files, they do not reload the open pages. /* custom.css */ :root { --dash-card: rgb(30 41 59 / 0.6); /* the card background */ } .card { border-radius: 12px; } . // custom.js document.title = `${document.title} · lab`; . The page’s colours are CSS variables on :root (--dash-bg, --dash-card, --dash-text, --dash-muted, --dash-accent, --dash-ok, --dash-warn, --dash-error, …), set for the light and the dark theme. Override them in custom.css for a theme of your own. Class names of the page may change between versions; variables are the steadier hook. Both files are your own code on your own page: the page’s Content Security Policy allows them like the page’s own script. Only put in what you trust. Inline scripts do not run: custom.js cannot add a <script> with code in it or an onclick="..." attribute; put the code in custom.js itself and use addEventListener.

194.title: Decisions
194.content: Why things are the way they are. Newest first.

195.title: The settings page writes the config files (2026-11-06)
195.content: Everything in the YAML files is to be managed from the settings page, so hard rule 5 (“the user’s files are never written”) became “only on an admin’s explicit save”. The app still never writes a config file on its own. Every save goes through src/config/edit.js: only the config files themselves, checked the way loadConfig loads them (a save that adds errors is refused), a 409 when the file changed since the page read it, and the previous version kept under .history/ (the last ten per file) so a mistake can be undone. The YAML Document API keeps comments, !include and variables as written.

196.title: Root scripts through one sudo rule, off by default (2026-10-25)
196.content: Scripts that maintain the homelab (swag configs) write files that must stay owned by root, and the dashboard runs as node. The server itself stays unprivileged (see the pitfalls); instead the image’s entrypoint, which starts as root anyway, can write one sudo rule that lets node run a fixed runner, /usr/local/bin/dashboard-root, which is bash as root. It does so only with DASHBOARD_ALLOW_ROOT_SCRIPTS=true, because the rule cannot tell the button from any other widget code. sudo -n never waits for a password; -E keeps the environment only with the button’s inheritEnv. A timeout reaches the root processes through sudo, which passes SIGTERM to the runner, and the runner stops its whole process group (node cannot signal root processes itself). Considered: running scripts in the webhook container through docker exec (works, keeps a second container), and ACLs (owner stays root, but shfs on Unraid does not support them).

197.title: Widgets may run actions; the button widget runs scripts (2026-10-25)
197.content: A separate webhook container ran the homelab’s scripts (bash with curl, jq and docker). The widget API got action(ctx) so a widget can do something on a press, and the collection’s button widget uses it to run a script file or an inline command in the dashboard container (bash, curl, jq, docker-cli and compose are in the image for it). The script is the user’s own code, from the config, never from the request; it runs as node with an empty environment unless the button says inheritEnv: true, and its output passes the secret scrubbing. The hard rules are about the dashboard’s own code: its Docker calls stay GET-only (rule 9) and it writes only its plugins folder (rule 5); what a configured script does with the socket or files is up to the user. There is no login, so anyone who can open the page can press the button: that is the user’s choice (documented in the widget’s README and in security.md). One action at a time per instance, at most an hour; the button keeps its own timeout (5 minutes by default).

198.title: Every widget in the widgets collection (2026-10-25)
198.content: The dashboard had built-in widgets: the generic and header ones, and the ones behind a service’s siteMonitor:, ping:, container:, app: and proxmoxNode:. They moved to the widgets collection, so a widget has one place, one release cycle and one test suite, and the dashboard is only the core. The core still creates those five widgets by id and fills in their options (CORE_WIDGETS in src/plugins/installer.js); their ids and options are a contract with the collection. The price: the first start needs network access to download the collection (the lock file covers later starts), the five run in the worker thread like any installed widget, and only: on the collection gets them added so the service fields keep working.

199.title: One worker thread for installed widgets (2026-10-24)
199.content: A widget’s fetch used to run in the dashboard’s event loop, so a loop without end froze the whole page and a leak took the process down, against hard rule 4. Installed widgets now run in a worker thread with resourceLimits; a call that ignores its timeout gets the worker terminated and started again. One worker for all of them rather than one per widget: a worker costs about 10 MB, and a homelab easily uses thirty widget types. Built-in widgets stay in the process (they are ours and some, like docker, are called very often). It is not a sandbox for hostile code: a worker has the same network and files.

200.title: Frames only for the configured origins (2026-10-24)
200.content: homepage’s iframe widget needs frame-src to allow the framed page. A blanket frame-src * would let any injected markup frame anything; instead widget.yaml names the options that hold a framed URL (frames: [src]), and the page’s CSP lists only the origins of their public values. Without an iframe widget the page keeps frame-src 'none'; API responses always do.

201.title: Webhooks through the server, not a hidden frame (2026-10-24)
201.content: homepage’s target: hidden-iframe loads a webhook in an invisible frame, which can never tell whether it worked, and needs a permissive frame-src. The dashboard server now calls the URL (only URLs from the config, never from the request; same header check as plugin sync) and the page shows “done” or the reason it failed. The CSP is back to frame-src 'none'.

202.title: Accessibility over a pixel-exact homepage copy (2026-10-24)
202.content: An audit against Apple’s HIG found homepage’s 8px status labels, 80%-opacity status colours (2.8:1) and thin weights below the minimums. The look stays homepage’s; the sizes, weights and colours follow the minimums, and tests/design.test.mjs checks them from the CSS. The appearance switch got an “auto” position because a two-way switch could never return to following the system.

203.title: homepage compatibility as a migration path (2026-10-23)
203.content: The first real installation replaces a homepage. Reading homepage.* labels, {{HOMEPAGE_VAR_*}}, homepage’s widget keys (refreshInterval, fields, hide_errors) and its look means a homepage setup moves over without relabelling containers or renaming secrets. The homepage-specific widgets (radarr, unraid, …) still live outside this repository, in a collection, to keep the core small and to prove the plugin model.

204.title: Several status labels per service (2026-10-23)
204.content: homepage shows a label per check (site monitor, ping, container). A single dot hid which check failed, so statuses is a list and each check is its own widget instance.

205.title: Path checks on resolved paths (2026-10-23)
205.content: /widgets/<id>/assets/..%2Fserver.js passed a “starts with assets/” check on the raw path. Every check is now done on the result of safeJoin, and a test covers the traversal.

206.title: HEAD is answered like GET (2026-10-23)
206.content: The http-status widget uses HEAD. The dashboard monitoring itself showed “degraded” because only GET was routed.

207.title: Widgets run in-process (2026-10-23)
207.content: A worker_thread per widget would limit memory and isolate crashes, but not network or file access (Node has no per-thread permissions). For v1 the trust model is explicit (security.md) and every call has a timeout. Workers are on the to-do list for resource isolation.

208.title: Status checks are widgets (2026-10-23)
208.content: siteMonitor, ping and container map to the http-status, ping and docker widgets. The status dot and widgets then share one runtime, cache and error handling, and a third-party widget can serve as a status check by returning status.

209.title: A log file only with logpath (2026-10-24)
209.content: homepage writes a log file into the config folder by default. Hard rule 5 keeps the app out of the user’s files, so here the log goes to stdout (docker logs) unless logpath asks for a file; then the rotation is homepage’s (10 MiB, five files) and LOG_TARGETS works the same.

210.title: The version is shown by default, as in homepage (2026-10-25)
210.content: At first the version was hidden unless hideVersion: false (2026-10-24: the HIG audit called it noise for the people using the page). Since every widget comes from the widgets collection, the footer also tells which collection release runs, which matters when something looks off; so the version is shown again by default, as in homepage, and hideVersion: true hides it. The update check (once a day, GitHub’s newest release) runs only while the version is shown, and never with disableUpdateCheck.

211.title: A mounted Docker socket works without a proxy (2026-10-24)
211.content: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock is what people try first, and it used to fail with EACCES because the image ran as node. The entrypoint now starts as root, adds node to the socket’s group and drops to node (su-exec) before anything else runs; with no servers in docker.yaml the mounted socket is used as local. The docker-socket-proxy stays the recommendation: :ro does not limit the Docker API, and widget code runs in the same process.

212.title: The widgets collection is always installed (2026-10-24)
212.content: Radarr, Sonarr, Unraid and the rest should work without first finding and adding a plugin source. The collection stays a separate repository (its own releases, the same contract as any third-party package), but DEFAULT_PLUGINS installs it at #latest, locked like any source. Listing the repository in settings.yaml replaces the default, to pin it or use only:. Bundling it in the image was rejected: every widget release would need a new image.

213.title: Lock file instead of always fetching (2026-10-23)
213.content: A start must not depend on GitHub or npm being reachable, and must not silently pick up new code. plugins.lock.yaml records the commit or integrity; ?update=1 moves floating refs. #latest is resolved to a release tag once and locked like one, so it saves users from editing a version without picking up code on a restart.

214.title: Node.js without a build step, one runtime dependency (2026-10-23)
214.content: Widget authors write the server and client in the same language. yaml is the only runtime dependency: YAML is the core of the configuration, and a hand-written parser is not worth the bugs. Docker and Kubernetes are reached with node:http(s), so no SDKs are needed.

215.title: Blocks as the default rendering (2026-10-23)
215.content: Most widgets show a few numbers. With declarative blocks they need no browser code, look consistent, and cannot break the page. client.js (a Web Component in shadow DOM) is the escape hatch.

228.title: Development
228.content: Requirements: Node.js 22+, git. Docker for the image. npm ci npm test # node:test, all files in tests/ npm run dev # http://localhost:3000 with config.example node src/server.js --config ~/my-test-config --port 3001 . | The tests load every widget from a checkout of the widgets collection: clone it next to this repository (../dashboard-widgets) or point DASHBOARD_COLLECTION_DIR at one. | The YAML reloads on save; changes to src/ or public/ need a restart. public/index.html only needs a browser refresh. | tests/helpers.mjs has tmpDir, writeWidget, serve (HTTP on a port or a unix socket) and fakeCtx for calling a widget’s fetch directly. | Fake Docker and Kubernetes responses live in tests/fixtures/. | .

229.title: Screenshots
229.content: The README and home page screenshots are made from the showcase config in scripts/showcase/. Its widgets ask the widgets collection’s fake homelab (scripts/mock-homelab.mjs in the collection, answering from its fixtures); status checks and system resources are stubbed, so the pictures are the same on every run: . npm install --no-save playwright && npx playwright install chromium node scripts/screenshots.mjs . The example image on each widget’s page is made the same way, from the example in the widget’s README, by scripts/widget-images.mjs while the site is built. To look at them locally: . node scripts/widget-images.mjs /tmp/widget-images . The collection’s scripts/fakes.mjs adds what its tests use too: fake services for widgets that speak something else than HTTP with JSON (apcupsd, game servers, My.JDownloader, …) and the options each widget needs for its fixture. A widget whose README example gets no data is tried again with those options. The iframe and MJPEG widgets show a made-up page and camera picture, and the browser’s clock is fixed in October 2026, the month of the calendar fixture.

243.title: Docker container
243.content: type: docker · version 1.8.0 · widget API 2 · Widget collection develop · source . State, CPU and memory of one container. This is the widget behind a service’s container:, which reads the server from docker.yaml; used directly, it takes a socket or a url. The dashboard only reads from Docker. Give it a docker-socket-proxy with CONTAINERS=1 rather than the socket itself: see Discovery. A Docker daemon over TLS (port 2376) is set up in docker.yaml with tls: { caFile, certFile, keyFile } (see Configuration); the dashboard fills in tlsCa, tlsCert and tlsKey for container: from those files. With swarm: true (set from docker.yaml’s swarm: true for container:), a name that is no container is looked up as a Swarm service: its running tasks against the replicas (replicas), marked when only some run. attention is true while the container is unhealthy (its Docker healthcheck), stopped or not found, so a service can hide its card while all is well: filter: container.attention == false reads it from the service’s container:.

PEM text; filled in from docker.yaml tls.caFile | . | tlsCert | string |   |   | Secret: stays on the server. PEM text; filled in from docker.yaml tls.certFile | . | tlsKey | string |   |   | Secret: stays on the server. PEM text; filled in from docker.yaml tls.keyFile | .
